title: US Plans to Cut Off Iran’s Caspian Lifeline
content:
US Central Command announced a plan on November 8 to block Iran’s land-based supply lines, building on its months-long naval blockade of the Islamic Republic’s ports. The goal of Task Force Iron Gate is to prevent Tehran from using alternative routes to transport advanced weapons, dual-use materials, and energy products.

Since the US and Israel started an all-out war on Iran in February and subsequently blockaded the Strait of Hormuz, Tehran has increasingly looked to northern corridors, particularly through Russia, to maintain access to foreign markets and critical supplies. The shift has elevated the importance of the Caspian route and forced Washington to take additional measures. 

Despite on-again, off-again negotiations between the US, Iran and intermediaries seeking to end the war, which has rattled global markets and sent inflation soaring. There is little sign of a resolution.

While Tehran has been able to rely primarily on its domestic defense industry for weapons production, it is increasingly looking to the north for imports, with the Caspian corridor emerging as a key route for defense-related procurement and logistical support.

title: AI’s Back Door to Finance
content:
Imagine asking an AI assistant to find you a better mortgage, compare your pension investments, and move your savings to an account offering a higher return. With your permission, it examines your finances, identifies better deals, and acts. No forms, no lengthy comparisons, no switching between banking apps. Just a digital assistant working in your financial interests.

This is the promise of agentic AI: technology that can make decisions and carry out tasks, making financial services more innovative, competitive, and affordable. There is one major obstacle: access to financial data.

In its 2027 work program, the European Commission announced plans to withdraw its proposed Financial Data Access Regulation (FIDA). FIDA represented Europe’s ambitious attempt to open up financial data beyond banking, allowing customers to give third parties access to their savings, investment, insurance, and pension accounts.

AI is already transforming personal finance. In the US, OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Anthropic’s Claude, and Google’s Gemini permit consumers to connect with their financial accounts and ask questions about their finances. Although these services have yet to launch in Europe, they are coming.

title: Russia Launching Near-Daily Attacks Across Europe
content:
Mass-casualty plots in NATO’s eastern borderlands, cruise missiles fired into allied countries, and intelligence agency warnings of more to come demonstrate a widening and more reckless pattern in Russia’s shadow war against European democracies.

The risks are rising with it. NATO countries met after one incident in Poland, but the collective allied response looks weak and uncertain. The larger European states are offering support, but the US is notably less vocal in response to Russian hostile acts, both proven and suspected. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in September that the risk of hybrid attacks metastasizing into open conflict was “a real concern”, but did not point the finger at Russia.

There is a clear danger that an incident may cause casualties in an allied state, and the response at that point is unclear. Russian strategy is to keep pushing until it meets resistance, and that moment has not arrived. Meanwhile, the Kremlin responds to the defensive measures of allied states by suggesting “open war” is nearing.

title: Kremlin Campaign to Crush Kaliningrad’s Identity
content:
Kaliningrad Regional Court sentenced lawyer and human rights defender Maria Bontsler to 12 years in prison for treason on November 12, after she was accused of passing information to Ukrainian intelligence. Bontsler’s real crime has been defending local people from political prosecutions.

The verdict was the latest step in a two-decade campaign to ensure Kaliningrad, Russia’s westernmost territory, has no independent political life.

For NATO planners, the exclave is a problem of missile ranges and the Suwałki Gap, the narrow strip on the border between Poland and Lithuania which links Kaliningrad to Belarus. For the Kremlin, weaponization of the territory is made easier by the absence of any civic movement that questions it.

It wasn’t always this way. Back in 1993, Sergey Pasko founded the Baltic Republican Party (BRP), which had influence beyond its list of barely 500 formal members.

title: China Sends Post-Shenzhen Signals to Europe
content:
Europe was left out of the Shenzhen summit, but it wasn’t forgotten, at least in Chinese minds. The state media was quick to send signals that it was thinking of Europe (which in turn has been thinking of targeting Chinese imports).

Xi Jinping’s November 19 appearance with US President Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin, the Russian leader, ended with a statement speaking of peace and co-operation in broad terms.

There was little for diplomats to get their teeth into beyond the images of the US and Chinese leaders standing together, accompanied by the head of a lesser Eurasian power. Europe was absent, and yet Beijing’s messaging suggests it still matters a great deal.

The Chinese party-state is adept at using its coordinated media outlets for coded dispatches in the absence of official position-taking. As initial clues to what comes next, these are worth noting because they serve as a guide to official thinking.

title: ITU Shatters Glass Ceiling
content:
It’s a momentous breakthrough: in a stunning upset, Estonia’s Nele Leosk unseated incumbent Zimbabwe’s Cosmas Zavazava in the election to become the Director of the ITU’s Development Bureau. Leosk joins re-elected American Secretary-General Doreen Bogdan-Martin, previously the only woman ever elected to an ITU leadership post. 

Beyond the gender revolution, the victories of American and Estonian women leave democratic nations in control of ITU leadership. Bahrain’s Adel Darwish (Deputy Secretary-General), Japan’s Seizo Onoe (Standardization), and France’s Eric Fournier (Radiocommunication) fill out the top team. 

Their victories are important for an open, free Internet. Despite strained transatlantic relations, Europe and the Trump Administration are cooperating in this one important international institution. Overt battles over Internet governance appear to be fading between the democracies and authoritarian Russia and China. The ITU can concentrate on the less explosive, but crucial tasks of bringing Internet access to the unconnected 26% of the global population in an affordable, sustainable fashion.

title: Populists vs. Protesters: Czechs Fight Over Public Broadcasters
content:
For much of the year, Letná Plain has nothing to offer either locals or tourists. 

It’s a large, featureless patch of land opposite the Sparta Prague football stadium. The surface alternates between dust and mud; there’s a car park for buses, and sometimes a circus. 

But every so often, Letná hosts an event that can tilt the world of Czech politics on its axis. Sometimes a little. Sometimes a lot. 

On Saturday, November 25, 1989, around 750,000 people gathered to demand the end of Czechoslovakia’s communist regime. The following day, many returned, and on Wednesday, November 29, parliament abolished the Communist Party’s leading role in society.  

Nothing like that is going to happen this time around, but on Sunday, November 15, there were perhaps 400,000 people on Letná for the largest demonstration in Prague since the Velvet Revolution.  

It looked huge when viewed from a media platform overlooking an ocean of flags and faces.  

The people who had gathered in the tens of thousands were there to protest against government plans to scrap the $10 monthly license fee which funds the nation’s two public broadcasters, Czech TV and Czech Radio.
snippet: For much of the year, Letná Plain has nothing to offer either locals or tourists.

title: Poland Foils Russian ‘Mass Casualty Plot’
content:
For months, Western intelligence agencies have warned that Russia might stage a major provocation that could escalate into a grave confrontation with NATO. Poland now believes it has thwarted precisely such a plot. 

According to a November 18 investigation by the Polish newspaper Rzeczpospolita, which cited unnamed senior sources connected to Poland’s security services, Russian intelligence was preparing a bloody false-flag operation near the border with Kaliningrad, the Russian exclave on Poland’s northeastern border.  

The plan was to stage an attack, possibly on Russian soil, causing mass casualties and planting evidence implicating Ukraine, with Poland portrayed as the base from which the attackers had struck. 

This aimed to drive a wedge between Kyiv and one of its staunchest allies, leaving Poles furious that Ukraine had supposedly dragged their country into a confrontation with Russia. 

Moscow could then have used the incident as a pretext to strike back, although it remains unclear where the bloodshed might have occurred.

title: CEPA Mourns the Loss of Ambassador Eric Rubin
content:
CEPA mourns the loss of Ambassador Eric Rubin, whose contributions to the cause of democracy and freedom, both within and outside government, stand as a testament to the power of thoughtful, dedicated public service. 

Across decades of service, most notably as US Ambassador to Bulgaria and Deputy Chief of Mission in Moscow, Ambassador Rubin brought unwavering integrity and deep diplomatic acumen to international relations. Throughout his distinguished career with the US Department of State, he served as a clear voice for democratic values while playing a pivotal role in strengthening transatlantic alliances and advancing regional stability. 

His influence extended meaningfully to policy analysis and strategic dialogue, including valuable contributions as a senior fellow to CEPA’s work. His investment in the next generation of leaders who benefited from his wisdom and experience made an especially valuable impact. Colleagues who had the privilege to work with him appreciated his warmth, sharp intellect, and collaborative spirit.

title: Protecting Norway’s Gas From Russia
content:
In any direct confrontation, European critical infrastructure would almost certainly become a target of the Kremlin’s long-range strikes, as it sought to degrade the continent’s warfighting capacity and population’s will to resist. 

One underappreciated vulnerability in Europe’s economic system is Norway’s natural gas infrastructure. Since 2022, Norway has replaced Russia as the continent’s main supplier, delivering 89 billion cubic meters to the European Union in 2025, almost one-third of the bloc’s gas imports and more than half of its pipeline supply. 

Russia’s share of EU gas continues to decline, while geopolitical volatility is making several other non-EU suppliers, foremost the US, less attractive. Norway’s role can be expected to grow further, both in its share of supply and political weight. 

Dependence on Norwegian gas is particularly high in Germany, the continent’s industrial powerhouse, whose factories are critical to European rearmament. In 2025, Norway supplied 44% of German gas imports, and industrial customers accounted for 60% of German gas consumption.

title: NATO Needs Joint Solution to Critical Minerals Threat
content:
This is part of a series examining the central importance of critical minerals and the race to ensure Western supply.

Multiple US government agencies released a series of funding vehicles and new policies in August as part of efforts to build a reliable, non-Chinese, critical minerals supply chain for defense production. The announcements received relatively little fanfare outside the trade and business media, yet their ambitious goal is to reshape global supply chains.

China has spent decades developing an industrial ecosystem “from soup to nuts” controlled by the Communist Party. It built an integrated natural resource supply chain, financing system, production industry, trained labor force, and large domestic market as it pursued modernization and national security.

The US and Europe now see China’s dominance in critical minerals as a Western national security vulnerability. Without the minerals and rare earths China supplies, modern defense technology cannot be made at scale in the near term.

title: An Icelandic Home Guard to Help Secure the North Atlantic
content:
The sparsely populated and remote island was a founding member of NATO in 1949, and is unique amongst the alliance’s members as it has no military. It relies instead on a bilateral defense agreement with the US and serves the alliance by providing facilities for surveillance, transit, and monitoring operations.

But it cannot continue to depend on NATO assets to solve basic military tasks and provide surveillance forever, particularly from hostile powers which want to use its territory for hybrid and kinetic warfare. NATO is short of personnel and seeking more manpower to face the Russian threat. It’s time Iceland shouldered its weight.

The alliance’s anti-submarine and surveillance aircraft patrolling the Greenland-Iceland-UK gap, and the intelligence units that help to keep it safe need protection at their bases. Iceland also needs to safeguard transportation assets for routes between Europe and North America.

The island is not massive, but it is still a significant territory, more than double the size of Denmark and equal to the US state of Kentucky. Even if a part of its landmass is made up of glaciers and active volcanoes, it is still a considerable landmass.

title: Murder Is Love, Says Putin Preacher
content:
Lest you were wondering just why Mother Russia is killing large numbers of Ukrainian civilians — including babies, toddlers, and children — every day, her favorite crackpot philosopher has the answer.

No, it’s not because, as Vladimir Putin likes to say, Ukrainians are neo-Nazis hellbent on joining NATO and lobbing nukes at Russia. Nor is it because Ukrainians have banned the Russian language and culture (which would come as a surprise to Ukraine’s Russian-speaking Ukrainians).  

Instead, says Aleksandr Dugin, Mother Russia’s influential answer to the Nazi philosopher Alfred Rosenberg, it’s all because of her great love for Ukrainians. According to Dugin’s November 7 interview, love is the culprit: “We love you, we respect you,” he says to Ukrainians, “and even if we have to kill you, we shoot our own brothers and sisters in the heart, in the face, in the head.”
